title: Scientists find a possible weak spot in a top Alzheimer's risk gene
summary:
Alzheimer's disease slowly harms memory, thinking and behavior. It affects more than 7 million older adults in the United States. Scientists at Mount Sinai have found new clues about a gene called APOE4. It is the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's, which means people who carry it have a higher chance of getting the disease.

Researchers have known for years that blood vessels in the brain get weaker as Alzheimer's gets worse, especially in people who carry APOE4. What was less clear is why. Many people treated the damage to the brain's blood flow as a result of the disease, not something that might help drive it.

Two new studies, published in Cell and Cell Stem Cell, point to a different idea. In the first study, the team built a map of the cells in the blood vessels of the human brain. They found that APOE4 changed the behavior of pericytes. Pericytes normally help keep small blood vessels steady. With APOE4, they changed into cells that make scar tissue. This led to more amyloid, an abnormal protein, building up around the blood vessels. That could get in the way of blood flow.

The scientists also found that this process may be reversible. When they blocked a signal called TGF-β, pericyte coverage was restored, and there was less scarring and amyloid. They saw the same result in older mice that carry APOE4.

In the second study, the team used miBrains, which are three-dimensional human brain tissue made from stem cells. miBrains with APOE4 built up more of an abnormal protein called alpha-synuclein. The team also found cholesterol collecting inside astrocytes, which are support cells in the brain. The researchers say these findings reveal new targets for treatments.
why_it_matters: Alzheimer's affects many older adults and their families. Finding a part of the process that may be reversible gives scientists new ideas to test in the search for treatments.

A cell that makes scar tissue
A medicine that treats brain disease

questions.question: What did APOE4 do to pericytes in the study?
options: It made them grow into brand new neurons
It made them join together with stem cells
It made them carry much more oxygen
It changed them into cells that make scar tissue

options: Pericyte coverage was restored and scarring and amyloid went down
The brain tissue stopped growing in the lab
The blood vessels stopped carrying any blood
The mice quickly lost most of their memory
